title: Feasibility of omitting the unenhanced phase in CT angiography for acute aortic pathologies
content:
by Soo Buem Cho, Jieun Byun

Objectives

To evaluate the feasibility of a contrast-only computed tomography angiography (CTA) protocol versus a conventional multiphase protocol for detecting and characterizing acute aortic pathologies, and reducing radiation dose.

Materials & methods

This retrospective study included 160 patients who underwent multiphase CTA for evaluating acute aortic syndrome. Two readers independently evaluated 640 predefined aortic segments for the presence of aneurysms, dissections, intramural hematomas (IMH), and penetrating atherosclerotic ulcers (PAU). Non-inferiority was assessed using generalized estimating equations with a prespecified 5% margin. Inter-protocol and inter-reader agreements were calculated using Cohen’s kappa. Radiation dose also was compared.

Results

The contrast-only protocol demonstrated non-inferiority to the full protocol for detecting all major aortic pathologies, with all confidence intervals falling within the 5% margin. Detection rates were identical for aneurysms (33.6% vs. 33.6%; p = 1.000) and similar for dissections (15.6% vs. 15.9%; p = 0.500). Detection rates were slightly higher with the contrast-only protocol for IMH (5.8% vs. 5.0%) and PAU (5.8% vs. 4.7%), primarily reflecting false-positive interpretation. Interprotocol agreement was perfect for aneurysm shape and rupture status (kappa = 1.000) but lower for mural thrombus characterization (kappa = 0.703). The contrast-only protocol achieved a 32.1 ± 5.7% reduction in mean DLP and 32.4 ± 4.5% for CTDI vol (both, p < 0.001).

Conclusion

In patients with acute aortic pathology, a contrast-only protocol demonstrated non-inferior diagnostic performance to the full multiphase protocol, with comparable reader agreement and a 32% reduction in radiation dose. These findings suggest that omitting the unenhanced phase may be feasible in selected clinical scenarios, particularly in patients undergoing serial surveillance imaging, where cumulative dose reduction is a priority.
